title: AVL-JEPA: Preventing Causal Dynamics Information Collapse in Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture World Models

paper.title: AVL-JEPA: Preventing Causal Dynamics Information Collapse in Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture World Models
paper.abstract: Abstract Joint embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) predict future latent representations without reconstructing observations, enabling world models to focus on high-level semantic dynamics. However, a JEPA can preserve high dimensional visual information while discarding information about the physical consequences of actions. We call this failure mode causal dynamics information collapse and propose action-grounded vision-invariance latent (AVL) to prevent this collapse. We first use the executed action as an auxiliary dynamics anchor that encourages the model to preserve dynamics information, and then use a vision-invariance pathway which aligns perturbed and clean latent predictions without discarding dynamics information, forcing the model to fully understand and utilize causal dynamics information. We validate AVL on four robotic control tasks (TwoRoom, PushT, OGBench Cube, and Reacher), showing that it substantially improves success rates under visual perturbations while preserving clean-environment performance. We further evaluate physical consequence alignment, clean–noisy dynamics consistency, and the causal effect of targeted transition subspace erasure. Collectively, these results indicate that dynamic information causally relevant to planning is preserved from collapse under AVL.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: World models learn to predict how an environment evolves, providing a compact substrate for planning and control ( Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018 ) . Joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) offers one way to achieve this goal. Instead of reconstructing future observations, a JEPA model predicts future latent representations directly ( Assran et al., 2023 ) . This design sidesteps pixel-level reconstruction and focuses on learning abstract predictive structure, making it attractive for world modeling. A central challenge in JEPA training is preventing representation collapse, where all inputs map to a narrow region of latent space. Existing work addresses this at the representation level: variance, covariance, and distributional regularizers penalize degenerate latent statistics ( Bardes et al., 2022 ) ; EMA-based teacher networks provide a slowly moving prediction target that resists instantaneous collapse ( Assran et al., 2023 ; Bardes et al., 2024 ) ; JEPA world models such as LeWM combine joint-embedding prediction with SIGReg regularization to prevent geometry-degenerate latent embeddings ( Maes et al., 2026 ; Balestriero & LeCun, 2025 ) . These mechanisms are effective at preventing global collapse and make the learned representations remain high dimensional, non-constant, and predictive on average. However, preventing global collapse does not guarantee that the latent preserves the information needed to distinguish how different actions causally change the physical state. Two distinct actions that produce different physical state changes may yield nearly identical predicted latent transitions. We refer to this failure as causal dynamics information collapse . We introduce action-grounded vision-invariance latent (AVL) to mitigate this collapse. The action-grounded pathway treats the real action as an auxiliary dynamic anchor, forcing the model to preserve enough dynamic information. The vision-invariance pathway then exposes the model to clean and visually perturbed observations while freezing the action head. The perturbed latent is aligned with the clean latent, but the action loss prevents this alignment from being achieved by simply discarding information, making the model fully use causal dynamics information to predict the future latent. Figure 1: Measured PCA projection of predicted Δ ​ z \Delta z transition responses for LeWM and AVL (ours). Both panels use one shared transform and identical action candidates; different colors denote different candidate action categories. Our method substantially mitigates causal dynamics information collapse and improves closed-loop planning performance. On TwoRoom, we lift predicted-to-physical consequence alignment (Spearman ρ \rho ) from 0.35 0.35 to 0.53 0.53 and reduce normalized regret from 0.152 0.152 to 0.061 0.061 , while clean–noisy ranking consistency increases from 0.89 0.89 to 0.98 0.98 . In closed-loop planning, success rate under Gaussian policy input noise ( σ = 0.10 \sigma{=}0.10 ) improves from 15.3 % 15.3\% to 81.5 % 81.5\% on PushT and from 65.7 % 65.7\% to 88.7 % 88.7\% on TwoRoom. Under saturation shift ( + 0.35 +0.35 ), it increases from 14.0 % 14.0\% to 62.0 % 62.0\% on PushT and from 54.8 % 54.8\% to 86.7 % 86.7\% on TwoRoom. We also improve OGBench Cube (from 73.2 % 73.2\% to 78.2 % 78.2\% under clean) and remain competitive on Reacher. These results suggest that global non-collapse is only a starting point, a useful world-model latent should preserve causal dynamics-relevant physical structure. Our main contributions are: • We formulate causal dynamics information collapse , a failure mode in which high dimensional visual latents insufficiently preserve action-conditioned physical change, and operationalize it with controlled experiments tied to physical outcomes. • We introduce action-grounded vision-invariance latent (AVL) that targets the collapse: the action-grounded pathway grounds state-conditioned latent transitions with executed actions to preserve dynamic information in latent space, and the vision-invariance pathway aligns perturbed and clean latents while freezing the action head, forcing the model to understand and utilize causal dynamics information to predict future latent. • We validate AVL across TwoRoom, PushT, Reacher, and OGBench Cube, showing that it substantially reduces success-rate degradation under Gaussian, brightness, and saturation perturbations while preserving clean environment performance, and provide mechanism-level experiments showing that the preserved dynamic information is causally meaningful.

sections.heading: Latent world models.
sections.text: World models learn a compressed simulation of the environment for planning and control ( Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018 ) . Early latent dynamics models reconstruct observations from learned states and train policies in latent imagination ( Hafner et al., 2019 ; Hafner et al., 2020 ; Hafner et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2023 ) . Reconstruction-free alternatives predict future latent features directly: DINO-WM plans on top of frozen DINOv2 features ( Zhou et al., 2025 ; Oquab et al., 2024 ) , PLDM combines joint-embedding prediction with VICReg-style collapse prevention and inverse dynamics ( Sobal et al., 2025 ) , and LeWM introduces SIGReg regularization for stable end to end training from pixels ( Maes et al., 2026 ; Balestriero & LeCun, 2025 ) .

sections.heading: Joint embedding predictive architecture.
sections.text: JEPA predicts target embeddings from context embeddings without pixel reconstruction and has become a prominent framework for self supervised representation learning ( LeCun, 2022 ; Assran et al., 2023 ) . A central challenge in JEPA training is representation collapse, where all inputs map to a narrow latent region. Early preventions rely on architectural asymmetry: I-JEPA uses an EMA target encoder and masked context prediction so that the context encoder cannot trivially copy the target ( Assran et al., 2023 ) . V-JEPA extends this to video with spatiotemporal masking ( Bardes et al., 2024 ) , and V-JEPA 2 scales the same recipe to large-scale video understanding and planning ( Assran et al., 2025 ) . Others use explicit statistical regularizers: VICReg penalizes latent variance, invariance, and covariance ( Bardes et al., 2022 ) , and LeJEPA provides a provable non-collapse guarantee through spectral regularization ( Balestriero & LeCun, 2025 ) . LeWM uses SIGReg to maintain non-degenerate latent statistics in world model ( Maes et al., 2026 ) , Sub-JEPA adds subspace Gaussian regularization ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) , and SD-JEPA decomposes the latent into progression and content subspaces ( Thil et al., 2026 ) . Concurrent works such as SMWM and Delta-JEPA expect inverse-dynamics method alone to prevent collapse. ( Ivashkov et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) . However, these methods mostly address collapse at the level of global latent statistics: variance, rank, covariance, or distributional non-degeneracy. Our work targets this gap: we study how to prevent the selective loss of causal dynamics information in JEPA world models, an information collapse directly limits model performance.

sections.heading: 3.2 AVL Overview
sections.text: Our method intervenes at two points in training. The action-grounded pathway establishes a clean dynamics-aware latent space using an action anchor. The vision-invariance pathway uses visual invariance as an alignment constraint: the latent transition predicted from a perturbed observation is aligned with the corresponding clean transition. Because the two views naturally differ, this alignment can be achieved either by preserving and utilizing the relevant causal dynamics or by discarding information until the two latent become similar. The frozen action head and its active loss rule out the latter shortcut, so the model is driven to infer state changes from causal dynamics. Figure 2: Overview of the proposed AVL method. The action-grounded pathway anchors clean latent transitions to executed actions through a transition-attributed action head that subtracts a state-only zero-transition baseline. The vision-invariance pathway aligns noisy and clean latent predictions while freezing the action head. The alignment creates a potential collapse shortcut, but the frozen action loss requires the latent to retain action-relevant dynamics, thereby targeting causal dynamics information collapse.

sections.heading: Tasks.
sections.text: We organize the study into four complementary experiments. Counterfactual physical consequence alignment (Figure 4 ) asks whether action anchoring improves alignment between latent transitions and physical consequences. Clean–noisy dynamics consistency (Table 1 ) tests whether clean–perturbed alignment with the frozen dynamics anchor preserves causal transition structure rather than collapsing it on both TwoRoom and PushT. Candidate-transition geometry and targeted erasure (Figure 5 ) examines the geometry of predicted candidate transitions and tests whether the directions used for consequence ranking are causally important by selectively removing them. Finally, closed-loop planning (Table 2 ) evaluates MPC performance to determine whether our model retains and utilizes causal dynamics information. We evaluate mechanism-level consistency on TwoRoom and PushT, and closed-loop planning on TwoRoom, PushT, Reacher, and OGBench Cube, following standard latent-world-model benchmarks and continuous-control suites ( Park et al., 2025 ; Tassa et al., 2018 ; Tunyasuvunakool et al., 2020 ) . Figure 4: Counterfactual physical consequence alignment, selection quality, and TwoRoom selection accuracy. The first panel reports predicted-to-physical Spearman correlation, the second reports normalized regret, and the third reports Top-1 and Top-3 selection accuracy. Higher Spearman and selection accuracy are better, whereas lower regret is better. Figure 5: Targeted erasure sweep on TwoRoom and PushT. Each panel reports the absolute difference between the erased and corresponding non-erased baseline values across k ∈ { 1 , 2 , 3 , 5 , 8 } k\in\{1,2,3,5,8\} for LeWM and AVL.

sections.heading: Experiment evaluation protocol.
sections.text: For closed-loop planning, each model is evaluated independently over 10 random seeds, with 50 episodes per seed. The action-grounded auxiliary action head uses a 256-dimensional hidden response and a task-specific output dimension d a d_{a} spanning H = 5 H=5 low level action steps. The auxiliary branch is saved separately and filtered from the weights used at evaluation, so planning uses the original LeWM architecture and interface with no additional modules. The remaining experiment evaluation protocols and metrics are detailed in Appendix B.1 .

sections.heading: Training configurations.
sections.text: We train on an NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPU. The action-grounded pathway is trained for 10 epochs with AdamW, learning rate 5 × 10 − 5 5\times 10^{-5} , weight decay 10 − 3 10^{-3} , bf16 mixed precision, and eight data loader workers. The vision-invariance pathway is initialized from action-grounded weights and trained for 2 epochs with AdamW, learning rate 10 − 5 10^{-5} , the same weight decay and precision, and batch size 128. Both pathways use λ 1 = 0.09 \lambda_{1}=0.09 for SIGReg, matching the original LeWM configuration, and λ 2 = 5 \lambda_{2}=5 for the action loss. On TwoRoom, the action-grounded sweep gives success rates of 85.2 % 85.2\% , 87.2 % 87.2\% , 92.8 % 92.8\% , and 92.6 % 92.6\% for λ 2 ∈ { 0.05 , 0.5 , 5 , 10 } \lambda_{2}\in\{0.05,0.5,5,10\} , respectively. This sweep supports the choice λ 2 = 5 \lambda_{2}=5 : increasing the action weight from 0.05 0.05 to 5 5 improves success by 7.6 percentage points, while λ 2 = 10 \lambda_{2}=10 does not improve further. In the vision-invariance pathway the action head is frozen while its loss remains active. The measured training time of both pathways is 41.7 minutes per epoch on PushT, 15.3 minutes per epoch on TwoRoom, 53.4 minutes per epoch on Reacher, and 61.9 minutes per epoch on Cube. Detailed training conditions are provided in Appendix B.6 .

sections.heading: Planning configuration.
sections.text: Closed-loop planning uses the LeWorldModel sampling-based planner with the default cross-task interface. The planner uses the cross-entropy method (CEM) with 300 candidate action sequences per iteration, 30 optimization iterations, and the top 30 candidates as elites. The prediction horizon, receding horizon, and action-block size are all 5; thus the planner predicts five action blocks and executes five low level actions before replanning. Goals are offset by 25 environment steps. Each seed is evaluated over 50 episodes, with a closed-loop execution budget of 50 environment steps per episode. The planning configuration is used for all model comparisons unless stated otherwise. sections.heading: 4.3 Clean–noisy dynamics consistency
sections.text: We analyze the collapse using the clean–perturbed quantities defined in Equations 14 – 16 . All quantities are first averaged across the three perturbation repeats for each state and then across states. Figure 3 visualizes the same-state nuisance/action geometry; red markers identify D nuis / D act > 0.5 D_{\mathrm{nuis}}/D_{\mathrm{act}}>0.5 together with a Top-1 flip. On TwoRoom, the vision-invariance pathway supplies the clean–perturbed alignment constraint while the frozen action loss prevents the model from discarding action-relevant variation. Relative to Action-grounded, clean–noisy Spearman increases by 0.0808 (95% CI [ 0.0646 , 0.0987 ] [0.0646,0.0987] ), same-top-1 frequency increases by 16.3 percentage points (95% CI [ 9.7 , 23.0 ] [9.7,23.0] ), nuisance drift decreases by 3.318 (95% CI [ − 3.579 , − 3.074 ] [-3.579,-3.074] ), and action-to-nuisance ratio increases by 0.899 (95% CI [ 0.840 , 0.960 ] [0.840,0.960] ). The independently repeated PushT protocol shows the same stability pattern: AVL has the highest clean–noisy Spearman and Top-1 agreement, the lowest nuisance drift, and the highest action-to-nuisance ratio. The simultaneous reduction in nuisance drift and retention of action separation is consistent with mitigating causal dynamics information collapse rather than uniformly suppressing latent variation.

sections.heading: 4.4 Counterfactual physical consequence alignment
sections.text: Figure 4 summarizes counterfactual physical consequence alignment across all four tasks. We report predicted-to-physical Spearman correlation and normalized regret, which directly measure whether the model orders candidate transitions according to their physical consequences and whether its selected candidate is close to the physical oracle. AVL improves both measures on TwoRoom, PushT, Reacher, and Cube in the aggregate view.

sections.heading: 4.5 Candidate-transition geometry and targeted erasure
sections.text: We apply the same k k -dimensional leading-subspace erasure procedure to both models following Equation 11 and compare the resulting changes in physical consequence ranking; a larger performance degradation for AVL indicates that its leading transition-response directions concentrate more information relevant to causal consequence. Figure 5 reports the complete k ∈ { 1 , 2 , 3 , 5 , 8 } k\in\{1,2,3,5,8\} sweep on TwoRoom and PushT. We report the absolute difference from each model’s corresponding non-erased baseline.

In Table 2 , the best result in each task column is bold and the second-best is underlined. Figure 7: Closed-loop OGBench Cube rollouts. The top row shows a successful AVL (ours) rollout, whereas the bottom row shows a failed LeWM rollout under the same task. Each row contains three temporally ordered agent observations and the corresponding goal observation. The full AVL (ours) pathway attains the highest success rate on TwoRoom and PushT across all four conditions and on Cube across all but the brightness shift. Figure 6 reports degradation relative to each model’s own clean performance. Another observation concerns generalization. The vision-invariance pathway is trained only with Gaussian noise on the policy input observation, yet the model also improves performance on brightness and saturation shifts, indicating the transfer is consistent with learning and exploiting causal dynamics information rather than merely fitting a specific augmentation.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We studied how to prevent causal dynamics information collapse in JEPA world models. Our AVL method uses action anchoring and constrained clean–perturbed alignment to preserve and exploit action conditioned physical structure. Counterfactual consequence ranking, clean–noisy consistency, targeted subspace erasure, and closed-loop transfer across unseen perturbations provide complementary evidence that the method effectively prevents this collapse.

sections.heading: Limitations and future work.
sections.text: AVL builds on the SIGReg regularizer of LeWM rather than replacing it, and we evaluate it only in simulation. We plan to remove the dependence on regularizers and to conduct real robot experiments in future work.

sections.heading: B.1 Mechanism-level protocols
sections.text: For the counterfactual experiment, we sample 100 matched simulator states and evaluate the same 12 candidate action sequences at every state, with each candidate spanning 5 action blocks. The simulator executes the shared candidate bank to obtain physical consequences. Spearman correlation and normalized regret measure ordering agreement and the physical cost of model selection; top- k k inclusion is reported as a secondary selection metric. For clean–noisy consistency, Gaussian noise with σ = 0.05 \sigma=0.05 is applied only to the current policy observation, while the physical rollout, goal, and success criterion remain clean; three noisy repeats are evaluated per state. Clean–noisy ranking consistency measures whether candidate ordering is preserved; nuisance drift measures perturbation-induced transition change at fixed action, and the action-to-nuisance ratio compares action-induced separation with that drift. Candidate-transition erasure uses the same predicted candidate responses and compares targeted removal of leading principal directions with random orthogonal removal.

sections.heading: B.2 Counterfactual protocol
sections.text: The archived mechanism experiment uses 100 matched simulator states and 12 shared candidate action sequences per state. Each candidate spans five action blocks, and each sequence covers 25 physical low level steps. Predicted latent responses, target latent responses, and two dimensional physical responses are saved for every state–candidate pair. Simulator restoration was audited over 1,200 renders per model with zero non-exact restorations and zero pixel difference. States are sampled from the held-out TwoRoom trajectory pool with a fixed seed; the shared action bank is reused for both models and consists of 12 sequences of five action blocks. Images use the model’s standard ImageNet normalization after any evaluation-time uint8 corruption. The physical oracle is the candidate with the largest physical response norm; regret is the oracle-minus-chosen response difference. All erasure branches rescore the same cached candidate responses.

sections.heading: B.3 PCA projection analysis
sections.text: Figure 1 is computed from archived TwoRoom counterfactual responses rather than from a conceptual drawing. For each of 100 matched simulator states, the same bank of 12 candidate action sequences is evaluated by LeWM , Action-grounded, and AVL. Each candidate contains five action blocks, corresponding to 25 low level environment steps. The plotted quantity is the predicted transition response Δ ​ z ^ = z ^ t + H − z t ∈ ℝ 192 \Delta\hat{z}=\hat{z}_{t+H}-z_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{192} , yielding an array of size 100 × 12 × 192 100\times 12\times 192 for each model. The action bank contains zero, cardinal, diagonal, and three smooth random candidate categories. Different colors in Figure 1 denote different candidate action categories; the individual category names are omitted from the main figure to keep the comparison visually compact. To make the two displayed panels directly comparable, we first concatenate all predicted transition responses from LeWM , Action-grounded, and AVL, standardize every latent dimension using one shared StandardScaler , and fit one two-component PCA transform to the resulting pooled matrix. We then project the LeWM and AVL responses through this same fitted scaler and PCA transform and display those two panels with identical coordinate limits. Action-grounded responses participate in fitting the shared transform to preserve the original three-model analysis protocol, but its panel is omitted from Figure 1 for clarity. The first two components explain 5.80% and 4.94% of the standardized variance, respectively. Because the projection retains only two of 192 dimensions, it is used as a qualitative visualization of transition-response organization, not as standalone quantitative evidence of physical consequence alignment or planning performance; those claims are evaluated using the counterfactual ranking, regret, erasure, and closed-loop results.

sections.heading: B.4 Perturbation protocol
sections.text: The clean–noisy consistency experiment applies Gaussian noise with σ = 0.05 \sigma=0.05 to the current policy observation only. The goal observation, simulator dynamics, physical consequence, and success criterion remain clean. Each state is evaluated with three noise repeats. The archived smoke audit contains paired clean/noisy policy input images, confirming that the perturbation is applied at the policy input. Noise is added to the policy input image in uint8 range [ 0,255 ] [0,255] before ImageNet normalization, with independent per-pixel IID sampling and a fixed corruption seed of 123; the goal observation is kept clean. A strict corruption audit over all conditions reported zero corruption failures. The additional evaluation settings use pure additive brightness shifts of + 0.10 +0.10 and + 0.20 +0.20 , and luminance-preserving saturation shifts of + 0.15 +0.15 and + 0.35 +0.35 , all applied to the current policy input while leaving the goal and physical rollout clean. Figure 8 visualizes these input-level transformations on one archived real PushT frame; it is illustrative and does not encode closed-loop success. The clean image is shown alongside the Gaussian, brightness, and saturation settings used in the evaluation protocol. These examples illustrate the appearance transformation only; they are not episode-level performance measurements.

sections.heading: B.5 Candidate-transition subspace erasure
sections.text: For each model, an operational PCA basis is fitted to centered predicted candidate-transition responses on 100 TwoRoom states, with 12 candidate action sequences per state and 5 action blocks per candidate. Before candidate scoring, the leading k k -dimensional subspace is removed and the candidates are rescored by the norm of the erased predicted transition. Figure 9 reports the complete, directly computed sweep k ∈ { 1 , 2 , 3 , 5 , 8 , 12 , 16 , 20 , 30 , 40 } k\in\{1,2,3,5,8,12,16,20,30,40\} for LeWM and AVL, with 10 same-dimensional random-subspace repeats as control. The targeted and random branches are evaluated from the same candidate responses; no interpolation or reconstructed aggregate values are used.

sections.heading: B.6 Main experiment training conditions
sections.text: The main LeWM training run was performed on AutoDL with an NVIDIA RTX 5090 (32 GB), a 14-vCPU Intel Xeon Gold 6348 CPU at 2.60 GHz, and the project’s ‘.venv‘ environment. The implementation used PyTorch 2.12.1+cu130 with its bundled CUDA 13.0 runtime, Lightning/stable-pretraining, bf16 mixed precision, Weights & Biases, and a local CSV logger. The data were split into 90% training and 10% held-out samples; image resolution was 224 224 , embedding dimension was 192, history size was 3, and one future prediction was trained. The optimizer was AdamW with learning rate 5 × 10 − 5 5\times 10^{-5} and weight decay 10 − 3 10^{-3} . Training used 11 epochs, batch size 128, 8 loader workers as specified by the training YAML, prefetch factor 3, pinned memory, persistent workers, bf16 precision, and gradient clipping at 1.0. The run summary recorded on the host additionally lists 12 workers; this is retained as an environment note rather than silently overwriting the versioned YAML setting. The SIGReg loss weight was 0.09, with 17 knots and 1024 projections. The checkpoint selected for evaluation was the final exported ‘lewm‘ checkpoint from the run; exact run identifiers and file hashes are retained in the accompanying experiment archive. These settings describe training-time configuration only; evaluation-time visual perturbations are applied separately at the policy input as specified in the perturbation protocol. Duan Huang Affiliation: Central South University Abstract Joint embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) predict future latent representations without reconstructing observations, enabling world models to focus on high-level semantic dynamics. However, a JEPA can preserve high dimensional visual information while discarding information about the physical consequences of actions. We call this failure mode causal dynamics information collapse and propose action-grounded vision-invariance latent (AVL) to prevent this collapse. We first use the executed action as an auxiliary dynamics anchor that encourages the model to preserve dynamics information, and then use a vision-invariance pathway which aligns perturbed and clean latent predictions without discarding dynamics information, forcing the model to fully understand and utilize causal dynamics information. We validate AVL on four robotic control tasks (TwoRoom, PushT, OGBench Cube, and Reacher), showing that it substantially improves success rates under visual perturbations while preserving clean-environment performance. We further evaluate physical consequence alignment, clean–noisy dynamics consistency, and the causal effect of targeted transition subspace erasure. Collectively, these results indicate that dynamic information causally relevant to planning is preserved from collapse under AVL. 1 Introduction World models learn to predict how an environment evolves, providing a compact substrate for planning and control ( Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018 ) . Joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) offers one way to achieve this goal. Instead of reconstructing future observations, a JEPA model predicts future latent representations directly ( Assran et al., 2023 ) . This design sidesteps pixel-level reconstruction and focuses on learning abstract predictive structure, making it attractive for world modeling. A central challenge in JEPA training is preventing representation collapse, where all inputs map to a narrow region of latent space. Existing work addresses this at the representation level: variance, covariance, and distributional regularizers penalize degenerate latent statistics ( Bardes et al., 2022 ) ; EMA-based teacher networks provide a slowly moving prediction target that resists instantaneous collapse ( Assran et al., 2023 ; Bardes et al., 2024 ) ; JEPA world models such as LeWM combine joint-embedding prediction with SIGReg regularization to prevent geometry-degenerate latent embeddings ( Maes et al., 2026 ; Balestriero & LeCun, 2025 ) . These mechanisms are effective at preventing global collapse and make the learned representations remain high dimensional, non-constant, and predictive on average. However, preventing global collapse does not guarantee that the latent preserves the information needed to distinguish how different actions causally change the physical state. Two distinct actions that produce different physical state changes may yield nearly identical predicted latent transitions. We refer to this failure as causal dynamics information collapse . We introduce action-grounded vision-invariance latent (AVL) to mitigate this collapse. The action-grounded pathway treats the real action as an auxiliary dynamic anchor, forcing the model to preserve enough dynamic information. The vision-invariance pathway then exposes the model to clean and visually perturbed observations while freezing the action head. The perturbed latent is aligned with the clean latent, but the action loss prevents this alignment from being achieved by simply discarding information, making the model fully use causal dynamics information to predict the future latent. Our method substantially mitigates causal dynamics information collapse and improves closed-loop planning performance. On TwoRoom, we lift predicted-to-physical consequence alignment (Spearman ρ \rho ) from 0.35 0.35 to 0.53 0.53 and reduce normalized regret from 0.152 0.152 to 0.061 0.061 , while clean–noisy ranking consistency increases from 0.89 0.89 to 0.98 0.98 . In closed-loop planning, success rate under Gaussian policy input noise ( σ = 0.10 \sigma{=}0.10 ) improves from 15.3 % 15.3\% to 81.5 % 81.5\% on PushT and from 65.7 % 65.7\% to 88.7 % 88.7\% on TwoRoom. Under saturation shift ( + 0.35 +0.35 ), it increases from 14.0 % 14.0\% to 62.0 % 62.0\% on PushT and from 54.8 % 54.8\% to 86.7 % 86.7\% on TwoRoom. We also improve OGBench Cube (from 73.2 % 73.2\% to 78.2 % 78.2\% under clean) and remain competitive on Reacher. These results suggest that global non-collapse is only a starting point, a useful world-model latent should preserve causal dynamics-relevant physical structure. Our main contributions are: • We formulate causal dynamics information collapse , a failure mode in which high dimensional visual latents insufficiently preserve action-conditioned physical change, and operationalize it with controlled experiments tied to physical outcomes. • We introduce action-grounded vision-invariance latent (AVL) that targets the collapse: the action-grounded pathway grounds state-conditioned latent transitions with executed actions to preserve dynamic information in latent space, and the vision-invariance pathway aligns perturbed and clean latents while freezing the action head, forcing the model to understand and utilize causal dynamics information to predict future latent. • We validate AVL across TwoRoom, PushT, Reacher, and OGBench Cube, showing that it substantially reduces success-rate degradation under Gaussian, brightness, and saturation perturbations while preserving clean environment performance, and provide mechanism-level experiments showing that the preserved dynamic information is causally meaningful. 2 Related Work Latent world models. World models learn a compressed simulation of the environment for planning and control ( Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018 ) . Early latent dynamics models reconstruct observations from learned states and train policies in latent imagination ( Hafner et al., 2019 ; Hafner et al., 2020 ; Hafner et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2023 ) . Reconstruction-free alternatives predict future latent features directly: DINO-WM plans on top of frozen DINOv2 features ( Zhou et al., 2025 ; Oquab et al., 2024 ) , PLDM combines joint-embedding prediction with VICReg-style collapse prevention and inverse dynamics ( Sobal et al., 2025 ) , and LeWM introduces SIGReg regularization for stable end to end training from pixels ( Maes et al., 2026 ; Balestriero & LeCun, 2025 ) . Joint embedding predictive architecture. JEPA predicts target embeddings from context embeddings without pixel reconstruction and has become a prominent framework for self supervised representation learning ( LeCun, 2022 ; Assran et al., 2023 ) . A central challenge in JEPA training is representation collapse, where all inputs map to a narrow latent region. Early preventions rely on architectural asymmetry: I-JEPA uses an EMA target encoder and masked context prediction so that the context encoder cannot trivially copy the target ( Assran et al., 2023 ) . V-JEPA extends this to video with spatiotemporal masking ( Bardes et al., 2024 ) , and V-JEPA 2 scales the same recipe to large-scale video understanding and planning ( Assran et al., 2025 ) . Others use explicit statistical regularizers: VICReg penalizes latent variance, invariance, and covariance ( Bardes et al., 2022 ) , and LeJEPA provides a provable non-collapse guarantee through spectral regularization ( Balestriero & LeCun, 2025 ) . LeWM uses SIGReg to maintain non-degenerate latent statistics in world model ( Maes et al., 2026 ) , Sub-JEPA adds subspace Gaussian regularization ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) , and SD-JEPA decomposes the latent into progression and content subspaces ( Thil et al., 2026 ) . Concurrent works such as SMWM and Delta-JEPA expect inverse-dynamics method alone to prevent collapse. ( Ivashkov et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) . However, these methods mostly address collapse at the level of global latent statistics: variance, rank, covariance, or distributional non-degeneracy. Our work targets this gap: we study how to prevent the selective loss of causal dynamics information in JEPA world models, an information collapse directly limits model performance. 3 Method 3.1 Causal Dynamics Information Collapse The JEPA prediction objective rewards information according to its predictability, which need not coincide with its causal relevance for control. Consequently, generic non-collapse constraints can maintain non-degenerate latent geometry without guaranteeing causal dynamics representations. 3.2 AVL Overview Our method intervenes at two points in training. The action-grounded pathway establishes a clean dynamics-aware latent space using an action anchor. The vision-invariance pathway uses visual invariance as an alignment constraint: the latent transition predicted from a perturbed observation is aligned with the corresponding clean transition. Because the two views naturally differ, this alignment can be achieved either by preserving and utilizing the relevant causal dynamics or by discarding information until the two latent become similar. The frozen action head and its active loss rule out the latter shortcut, so the model is driven to infer state changes from causal dynamics. Figure 2: Overview of the proposed AVL method. The action-grounded pathway anchors clean latent transitions to executed actions through a transition-attributed action head that subtracts a state-only zero-transition baseline. The vision-invariance pathway aligns noisy and clean latent predictions while freezing the action head. These quantities separate retained action-conditioned variation from perturbation-induced drift and directly test whether the frozen dynamics anchor preserves candidate geometry under visual corruption. 4 Experiments 4.1 Tasks and Metrics Tasks. We organize the study into four complementary experiments. Counterfactual physical consequence alignment (Figure 4 ) asks whether action anchoring improves alignment between latent transitions and physical consequences. Clean–noisy dynamics consistency (Table 1 ) tests whether clean–perturbed alignment with the frozen dynamics anchor preserves causal transition structure rather than collapsing it on both TwoRoom and PushT. Candidate-transition geometry and targeted erasure (Figure 5 ) examines the geometry of predicted candidate transitions and tests whether the directions used for consequence ranking are causally important by selectively removing them. Finally, closed-loop planning (Table 2 ) evaluates MPC performance to determine whether our model retains and utilizes causal dynamics information. We evaluate mechanism-level consistency on TwoRoom and PushT, and closed-loop planning on TwoRoom, PushT, Reacher, and OGBench Cube, following standard latent-world-model benchmarks and continuous-control suites ( Park et al., 2025 ; Tassa et al., 2018 ; Tunyasuvunakool et al., 2020 ) . Experiment evaluation protocol. For closed-loop planning, each model is evaluated independently over 10 random seeds, with 50 episodes per seed. The action-grounded auxiliary action head uses a 256-dimensional hidden response and a task-specific output dimension d a d_{a} spanning H = 5 H=5 low level action steps. The auxiliary branch is saved separately and filtered from the weights used at evaluation, so planning uses the original LeWM architecture and interface with no additional modules. The remaining experiment evaluation protocols and metrics are detailed in Appendix B.1 . 4.2 Implementation Details Training configurations. We train on an NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPU. The action-grounded pathway is trained for 10 epochs with AdamW, learning rate 5 × 10 − 5 5\times 10^{-5} , weight decay 10 − 3 10^{-3} , bf16 mixed precision, and eight data loader workers. The vision-invariance pathway is initialized from action-grounded weights and trained for 2 epochs with AdamW, learning rate 10 − 5 10^{-5} , the same weight decay and precision, and batch size 128. Both pathways use λ 1 = 0.09 \lambda_{1}=0.09 for SIGReg, matching the original LeWM configuration, and λ 2 = 5 \lambda_{2}=5 for the action loss. On TwoRoom, the action-grounded sweep gives success rates of 85.2 % 85.2\% , 87.2 % 87.2\% , 92.8 % 92.8\% , and 92.6 % 92.6\% for λ 2 ∈ { 0.05 , 0.5 , 5 , 10 } \lambda_{2}\in\{0.05,0.5,5,10\} , respectively. This sweep supports the choice λ 2 = 5 \lambda_{2}=5 : increasing the action weight from 0.05 0.05 to 5 5 improves success by 7.6 percentage points, while λ 2 = 10 \lambda_{2}=10 does not improve further. In the vision-invariance pathway the action head is frozen while its loss remains active. The measured training time of both pathways is 41.7 minutes per epoch on PushT, 15.3 minutes per epoch on TwoRoom, 53.4 minutes per epoch on Reacher, and 61.9 minutes per epoch on Cube. Detailed training conditions are provided in Appendix B.6 . Planning configuration. Closed-loop planning uses the LeWorldModel sampling-based planner with the default cross-task interface. The planner uses the cross-entropy method (CEM) with 300 candidate action sequences per iteration, 30 optimization iterations, and the top 30 candidates as elites. The prediction horizon, receding horizon, and action-block size are all 5; thus the planner predicts five action blocks and executes five low level actions before replanning. Goals are offset by 25 environment steps. Each seed is evaluated over 50 episodes, with a closed-loop execution budget of 50 environment steps per episode. The planning configuration is used for all model comparisons unless stated otherwise. Our AVL method uses action anchoring and constrained clean–perturbed alignment to preserve and exploit action conditioned physical structure. Counterfactual consequence ranking, clean–noisy consistency, targeted subspace erasure, and closed-loop transfer across unseen perturbations provide complementary evidence that the method effectively prevents this collapse.
